Where formula exceeds a given Gospel, the excess is likewise testimony. Mark 16:1–8 does not narrate an appearance. Paul does. Mark is not a denial of appearances. Paul is not a denial of the tomb-scene.

Thus:

> **Early formula and later narrative detail are two strata of one claim. The chapter uses both. It does not flatten them. It does not play them against each other as if the church had two Easters.**

---

# 46.28 The Empty-Tomb Narratives Without Illicit Dismissal

The empty-tomb narratives may now be examined as testimony of the place-claim.

**Common structure.** Women come early on the first day of the week. The stone is not where they expected. They find emptiness. They receive an announcement that He is risen and is not here. They are sent to the disciples. Appearances follow in Matthew, Luke, and John, and are already known to Paul.

**Particularity.** Spices, the hour, the question "Who shall roll us away the stone?", the young man or the angels, the linen, the napkin apart in John, the race of Peter and the other disciple — these are narrative particulars. They are the kind of particulars that belong to memory of a morning, or to skilled narrative, or to both. They are not required to be independently paralleled in Paul in order to be testimony.

**The women as first discoverers.** All four Gospels place women first at the tomb. Paul does not name them in the appearance-list of 1 Corinthians 15. The omission has been used to dismiss the tomb-stories as late. The use is illicit for two reasons. First, a compact list of official witnesses to appearances is not a chronicle of a morning's discovery. Second, the presence of women as primary tomb-witnesses in every Gospel is the opposite of a late apologetic improvement. A late improver constructing a case for a male-legal world would more naturally have Cephas find the tomb. The Gospels have Mary Magdalene. Paul has Cephas as first in the appearance-list. The two facts are compatible: women discover emptiness; Cephas is named as first among the official seers. They are not two Easters.

**Emptiness as a public-world claim.** A tomb either contained a body on the first day or it did not. The preaching in Jerusalem did not, on the record we have, include a pilgrimage to a venerated corpse. It included the proclamation that God raised Him. Matthew's rumour that the disciples stole the body (28:11–15) is, whatever one makes of Matthew's guard, evidence that the dispute was about a missing body, not about a missing mood.

The empty tomb does not, by itself, name the cause. The narratives name the cause: He is risen. The appearances name the cause as encounter. The formula names the cause as God's raising. The tomb-claim is one member of that conjunction. It is not to be dismissed because it is not the whole. It is not to be isolated as if emptiness without raising-speech were the Gospel.

---

# 46.29 Appearance Narratives: Jerusalem, Galilee, Named Persons, Physical Marks

The appearance-narratives have a geography and a physics.

**Jerusalem appearances.** Luke and John concentrate initial encounters in Jerusalem: the gathered disciples, Emmaus (near Jerusalem), Thomas, the locked room. Luke 24:47–49 and Acts 1:4 locate the commission and the waiting in the city of the death. Preaching begins there (Acts 2). The geography is the geography of publicity already named: the raising is announced where the crucifixion was known.

**Galilean appearances.** Mark 16:7 already promises, "he goeth before you into Galilee." Matthew 28:16–20 narrates a mountain there. John 21 narrates a lakeside. The ministry began in Galilee (Chapter 43). The raised Lord is claimed in the same land, not only in the feast-city. Two geographies are not two contradictions until they are forced into a single hour. Acts 1:3 speaks of many days. Multiple settings are what multiple days would produce.

**Named persons.** Mary Magdalene is not a type. Thomas is not a type. Cleopas is named (Luke 24:18). Peter runs. The beloved disciple believes upon seeing linen (John 20:8). Particular names are the opposite of allegory's preference for Everyman.

**Physical marks.** Wounds, feet held, fish eaten, breakfast cooked — these have already been cited against spiritual survival. They also bear upon hallucination as a global explanation. A shared inner vision does not ordinarily include a shared meal of leftover fish unless the meal is itself a vision, in which case the category "vision" has again become a solvent of every recalcitrant particular.

Luke 24:25–27, 44–47 records that the raised Jesus interprets Moses, the prophets, and the psalms as concerning His suffering and rising. That scene is the claim that the raised Lord Himself joined the event to the Scriptures. The full case of His confirmation of Scripture is Chapter 48. The scene is noted here because it is part of an appearance-narrative, and because the formula's "according to the scriptures" is not a Pauline hobby absent from the Gospels. The hinge includes that correspondence. The Graphē-gate is not hereby opened.

John 20:21–23 and Matthew 28:18–20 record commission: sending as the Father sent Him; all authority in heaven and earth; making disciples of the nations. Those commissions are the appearance-claim's movement into apostolic mission. Chapters 49–50 will examine apostolic authority. This chapter records that the appearances, as narrated, are not mere consolations. They are the origin-point of a public testimony the speakers will treat as binding.

Thus:

> **The appearance-narratives locate encounters in Jerusalem and Galilee, name persons, insist on bodily marks and table-fellowship, join the event to the Scriptures, and send witnesses. They are later written testimony of the formula's "he was seen," not a substitute religion of inner light.**

---

# 46.30 Acts: The Apostolic Proclamation as Death-and-Resurrection Testimony

Acts presents the public aftermath as preaching.

The speeches are not transcripts in the modern sense. They are Luke's orderly account of the kind of proclamation the witnesses made. Chapter 18 already treated Luke 1:1–4 as a claim of investigation. The present use is the content of the preaching as Luke presents it.

**Acts 2:22–36**, at Pentecost in Jerusalem, joins Chapter 45's works-axis to this chapter's object in one sermon. Jesus of Nazareth is a man approved of God by works known to the hearers. He was delivered, crucified, slain. God raised Him up, loosing the pains of death. David spoke of One whose flesh would not see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, whereof they are all witnesses. Being by the right hand of God exalted, He has shed forth the Spirit now seen and heard. Let all the house of Israel know that God hath made that same Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ.

The hinge is explicit. Works approve. Death occurs. God raises. Witnesses exist. Scripture is cited. Lordship is proclaimed. The sermon does not offer the ministry's signs as a stopping-place. It offers them as the known career of the man now preached as crucified and raised.

**Acts 3:13–15** names the denial before Pilate, the desire for a murderer, the killing of the Prince of life, "whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses."

**Acts 4:10, 33** repeats the name, the crucifixion, the raising, and adds that "with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus."

**Acts 5:30–32** names hanging on a tree, raising, exaltation, and "we are his witnesses of these things."

**Acts 10:39–41**, already cited, adds eating and drinking with Him after He rose.

**Acts 13:28–31**, in a synagogue of the diaspora, recites no cause of death found, Pilate's fulfillment of the request to slay Him, taking down from the tree, burial in a sepulchre, raising the third day, and appearance "many days unto them which came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses unto the people."

**Acts 17:31–32**, at Athens, names raising from the dead as the assurance God has given that the appointed man will judge the world, and records mockery at the resurrection of the dead. The hinge is still the hinge when the audience is Gentile and unpersuaded.

**Acts 26:8, 22–23**, before Agrippa, asks why it should be thought a thing incredible that God should raise the dead, and states that Moses and the prophets said that Christ should suffer and that He should be the first that should rise from the dead and show light to the people and to the Gentiles.

Across Jerusalem, Caesarea, diaspora synagogue, Areopagus, and a royal hearing, the proclamation is not a wisdom-school that happens to mention Jesus. It is testimony that the crucified was raised. Acts 1:21–22 had already made witness of His resurrection a qualification for the one who would take Judas's place. That qualification will belong to Chapters 47 and 49 as office and credibility. It belongs here as ranking: the resurrection is the fact an apostle must be able to attest.

Thus:

> **Acts presents apostolic preaching as death-and-resurrection testimony in public, at the scene and far from the scene, to Israel and to Gentiles. The witnesses themselves, as Luke presents them, treat this conjunction as the center of what they have to say.**

---

# 46.31 Significance for Apostolic Testimony: The Hinge the Witnesses Themselves Treat as Decisive

Significance, in this chapter, is not a homiletic improvement of the facts. It is the record's own ranking of the facts for the act of testimony.

The witnesses treat death-and-resurrection as decisive in at least six stated ways.

**As gospel-content.** 1 Corinthians 15:1–4: this is the gospel preached, received, stood in, saving if kept. Romans 1:3–4 names the same architecture in another letter: Jesus Christ made of the seed of David according to the flesh, "declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead." The identity Chapter 44 examined is here publicly declared in the raising. The raising does not create the Son. It declares Him.

**As the condition of their own truthfulness.** 1 Corinthians 15:15: if He is not raised, they are false witnesses of God. Testimony stands or falls with the event.

**As apostolic qualification.** Acts 1:21–22: one must be made a witness with them of His resurrection. The office is not "companion of a teacher" only. It is witness of this reversal.

**As the content of their power in public.** Acts 4:33: with great power they gave witness of the resurrection. The summary does not say they gave witness of Galilean aphorisms. It names the raising.

**As the article of confession.** Romans 10:9: "if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved." The verse is the word of faith as Paul preaches it. This chapter takes it as evidence of ranking, not as an entry into the Six First Principles. Salvation-speech in the letters already has the raising at its center.

**As the ground of hope.** 1 Peter 1:3: a lively hope "by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." 1 Thessalonians 4:14: "if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." The dead in the assemblies are not consoled by a metaphor. They are consoled by an analogy from an event.

Chapter 45's axis is not cancelled by this ranking. It is completed as history. Acts 2:22–24 is the grammar: approved by works, crucified, raised. The works interpret the claims. The death is the claims' crisis. The raising is the reversal the witnesses treat as God's verdict on the crucified.

Revelation 1:5 has already named Jesus Christ "the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead." The titles are adjacent. Witness and firstborn from the dead are not two careers. Chapter 44 used the faithful-witness title as identity. This chapter uses the adjacent title as the event that the witness-title now historically includes: the One who is the faithful witness is the One who was dead and is alive (Revelation 1:18).

The dedicated examination of how eyewitnesses function, and of how apostolic testimony carries authority, remains. The ranking is already in force:

> **Death-and-resurrection is the hinge the witnesses themselves treat as decisive for the truthfulness of their preaching, the content of their gospel, the qualification of their office, and the hope they offer. Movement VI cannot stop at Capernaum. The apostles did not.**

---

# 46.32 Why a Crucified Messiah Required This Hinge

The hinge is not arbitrary. A crucified Messiah is, in the world of Second Temple Judaism, a scandal, and in the Greek world a folly (1 Corinthians 1:23). Deuteronomy 21:23 hangs over a hanged man as curse. Messianic hope, in its ordinary public forms, did not run toward a prefect's cross at Passover.

Chapter 45 showed why the career runs toward that cross as interior logic. The present point is why the movement that survived the cross did not survive it as a memorial society for a dead prophet.

A dead prophet can be honoured. John the Baptist was honoured, and Josephus records him independently, and his disciples appear in Acts 19 still as a distinguishable group. The Jesus-movement is not presented as a memorial. It is presented as a proclamation that God has made the crucified both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36). That proclamation is unintelligible without the raising. With the raising, the cross is not the refutation of the claims. It is the claims' crisis reversed.

The ministry-predictions already required this reversal. "The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected … and be killed, and after three days rise again" (Mark 8:31). The predictions are claims of the career (Chapter 45). They come due in this chapter. A movement that remembered only the death would remember a failed prediction. A movement that proclaimed the raising proclaimed the prediction kept.

John 2:19–22 already stood on the edge: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The narrator interprets: He spoke of the temple of His body; the disciples remembered after He was raised. John 11:25 already named Him the resurrection and the life before He Himself entered death. Those edges are now the case. Identity with the Truth (Chapter 44) and authority over life in the ministry (Chapter 45) meet the public end and the claimed reversal.

Thus:

> **The hinge is required by the scandal of the cross, by the career's own predictions, and by the identity already claimed. Apostolic testimony treats the raising as God's public reversal of the public execution, not as an edifying appendix to a martyrdom.**

---

# 46.33 Competing Claim: Spiritual Survival or Immortal Soul

The reduction says:

> **What the apostles meant, or what happened in fact, is that Jesus' soul, cause, or presence continued. Bodily raising is later mythological clothing of a spiritual insight.**

The reduction fails for specified reasons.

First, **the earliest form already includes burial and raising of the buried, and appearance-language, and a third day**. Spiritual survival does not need a grave or a morning. The formula does.

Second, **Luke 24:37–43 and John 20:27 exist to refuse the disciples' own first reduction to "a spirit."** The testimony is not naïve about the alternative. It records the alternative and blocks it.

Third, **Paul's polemic in 1 Corinthians 15 is unintelligible as a defence of influence-survival**. Influence-survival would not make the witnesses false witnesses of God if it were all they meant. They meant that God raised Christ.

Fourth, **Jewish hope of resurrection, as Martha states it and as Daniel 12:2 frames it, is hope for the dead as raised, not hope that souls never die**. The Christian claim is that this hope has occurred in one man as firstfruits in the midst of history. That is a specification of resurrection, not a translation of resurrection into Platonism.

Fifth, **an empty tomb and a continuing soul can be true together only if the body is also missing for another reason**. The reduction that keeps the soul and discards the body must still explain the tomb-claim and the appearance-claim. It does not. It changes the object.

The apostles may also have believed that the dead in Christ are with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). That belief, whatever its full mapping, is not this chapter's object. This chapter's object is the raising of Jesus. Spiritual survival as a global explanation of Easter fails that object.

The reduction fails.

---

# 46.34 Competing Claim: Legend and Mythic Accretion

The reduction says:

> **A historical teacher was crucified. Stories of raising accrued as legend over decades. By the time of the Gospels, Easter is mythology. Even 1 Corinthians 15 is already legendary clothing.**

The reduction fails for specified reasons.

First, **Chapter 43 already destroyed the vacuum and the coreless legend**. A located man, a short public career, crucifixion under Pilate, a brother named James, a movement in the 50s — these remain. Accretion upon a core must then explain the content, the date, and the form of the resurrection clause.

Second, **the date is too early for the ordinary legendary century**. The formula is received, delivered at Corinth's founding, recited in the 50s, and overlapped with living named seers. Decades are not nothing. Decades are not centuries. A legend of bodily raising, burial, third day, and five hundred at once, among persons who had known the dead man, in the city of the execution and in assemblies that could ask Cephas and James, is not the ordinary drift of hero-romance.

Third, **the form is not the ordinary form of legend**. Legend typically smooths, removes friction, and accumulates wonders without the scandal of the cross as the message's center, without "some are fallen asleep," without Paul's shame as persecutor, without women fleeing in fear, without Thomas's refusal, without the stolen-body rumour as a live rival. The testimony retains challenge, doubt, shame, and rival explanation as structural moments. Inflation that produces 1 Corinthians 15:17 would ordinarily not stake forgiveness itself on a clause that could be denied in the assembly.

Fourth, **multiple streams carry the same sequential claim**. Pauline formula; Synoptic passion and emptiness; Johannine passion and encounters; Acts-preaching from Jerusalem to Athens. Independent idiom with the same architecture is the same evidential fact Chapters 43–45 used. Legendary inflation must then be multiple, early, and coincident, and must include a hostile Roman notice of the execution that the legend supposedly adorned.

Fifth, **the shame of crucifixion works against free inflation**. Chapter 43 already used that shame as historical weight for the death. A legend that wished only glory would more naturally omit the cross or transfigure it into a bloodless triumph. The movement preaches Christ crucified and raised. The combination is stubborn. Stubbornness is not a magic criterion. It is the observation that the legend-reduction must explain why the most awkward fact was kept as the center and then "solved" by an equally public raising rather than by a quieter spiritualization.

Sixth, **Movement V already warranted the writings as authentic testimony, not as late folklore**. Local growth of scenic detail remains a legitimate question. It is not a global solvent of the four-clause claim.

The community remembered, preached, and wrote. Memory is not the same act as the creation of a bodily raising out of a dead teacher within the lifetime of the brother, the pillars, and the persecutor-turned-preacher. The reduction fails as an explanation of the first-century claim.

---

# 46.35 Competing Claim: Hallucination as Global Explanation

The reduction says:

> **The disciples experienced grief-induced visions. Appearances are subjective. No bodily raising occurred. The tomb, if empty, has another explanation, or the tomb-stories are later.**

The reduction fails for specified reasons.

First, **it must be applied uniformly across a diverse class of claimed encounters, and the class resists uniformity**. Cephas; the twelve; more than five hundred at once; James the unbelieving brother; Paul the hostile persecutor; women at a tomb; two on a road; a meal of fish; a lakeside breakfast; days rather than a moment. Grief-consolation may be offered, with strain, for intimates in the first shock. It is not a natural account of a persecutor years into hostility, or of a brother who had not believed, or of five hundred at once. A family of ad hoc inner states is then named as one explanation. A family of ad hoc explanations is not one explanation.

Second, **simultaneity is not the ordinary mark of private hallucination**. "At once" in 1 Corinthians 15:6 is the formula's word. Mass grief can produce mass mood. It does not ordinarily produce a shared seeing of one person who speaks, commissions, and eats, unless the category has again become a solvent.

Third, **hallucination does not empty a tomb**. The reduction must therefore deny the tomb-claim, or add a second cause for emptiness, or both. The added cause is then a different reduction (theft, misidentification, non-burial) riding under the hallucination banner. Global explanation has split.

Fourth, **the physical particulars exist to be the sort of thing hallucination is not**. Handle me; flesh and bones; wounds; fish. The narratives may be dismissed wholesale, but then the reduction is no longer interpreting the testimony. It is replacing it. If the testimony is the object, the particulars belong to the object.

Fifth, **Paul's "last of all" seeing is dated to a man not grieving with the twelve in Jerusalem in the first days**. The persecutor is the wrong psychological subject for the standard grief-vision thesis. A special vision may then be granted to Paul and grief-visions to the others. The reduction has again split, and still has not explained James.

Sixth, **the reduction offers no account of the formula's burial-clause or of the public preaching in Jerusalem**. A city that could point to a body could refute a vision-gospel of raising. The record we have is not of a refutation by corpse but of a rumour of theft and of a proclamation that continued.

Some persons, in the world's ordinary course, do hallucinate. That fact does not become a solvent of this claim's diversity, dates, hostility-reversals, bodily marks, and tomb-sequence. The live question is whether the testimony is better explained as authentic proclamation of a bodily raising with appearances, or as a heap of inner events later captioned with graves and fish. The heap fails the mix of seers, the simultaneity, the tomb, and the argument of 1 Corinthians 15:15.

The reduction fails.

---

# 46.36 Competing Claim: Stolen Body

The reduction says:

> **The body was removed by disciples, or by some other human agency. Appearances are then fraud, or grief, or later legend built on the theft.**

The reduction is ancient. Matthew 28:11–15 records that this explanation circulated: the disciples came by night and stole Him while the guard slept. Matthew's narrative of bribes and of the saying being "commonly reported among the Jews until this day" is Matthean. What it establishes even for a reader who suspends the guard-story is that theft was a live rival explanation of emptiness in the world that produced the Gospel. The rival is therefore not a modern invention. It is to be answered as a first-century alternative.

The reduction fails for specified reasons.

First, **theft can, at most, explain emptiness**. It does not explain appearances to James and to Paul. It does not explain five hundred at once. It does not explain the transformation of the public message from a dead messianic claimant into the proclamation that God raised Him, under the threat the same authorities still posed. Theft plus hallucination is then required, or theft plus fraud. The reduction is no longer simple.

Second, **fraudulent theft by the inner circle makes the witnesses false witnesses of God in the exact sense 1 Corinthians 15:15 names**, and makes them false witnesses who then suffered for the falsehood. Acts presents arrest, beating, and, in later narrative, death. Motive for a sustained, costly fraud is not supplied by grief for a dead teacher. Grief buries and remembers. It does not ordinarily steal a corpse in order to preach a raising under the Sanhedrin's nose and then include "for our sins according to the scriptures" as the first clause.

Third, **the women-as-discoverers and the disciples' recorded unbelief sit poorly with a planned theft**. A planned fraud would more naturally have produced a coordinated, immediate, male announcement. The narratives have fear, doubt, slow recognition, and a rumour from the women that sounded as idle tales (Luke 24:11). Fraud that writes its own incompetence into the opening of the story is not the ordinary fraud.

Fourth, **Joseph's known tomb is the wrong object for a quiet removal that leaves no controversy**. The controversy Matthew attests is the controversy emptiness would produce. A body remaining in a known place would have been the simpler refutation. The theft-story exists because a remaining body was not the explanation on offer in that dispute.

Fifth, **other human agencies** — grave-robbers, the gardener of John's 20:15, the authorities themselves — are sometimes proposed. Grave-robbers do not produce Easter preaching. A gardener's removal would be checkable in Jerusalem. Official removal would be a weapon against the preaching; it is not the weapon the speeches in Acts are recorded as facing. The recorded rival is theft by disciples. That rival fails the appearance-list and the cost.

Theft remains possible as a bare logical alternative to emptiness. Bare logical alternatives are not explanations of the conjunction this chapter has defined: emptiness plus early named appearances plus costly public proclamation that God raised the crucified. The reduction explains a strand and cancels the structure.

The reduction fails.

---

# 46.37 Competing Claim: Swoon / Apparent Death

The reduction says:

> **Jesus did not die. He fainted, was taken down, revived in the tomb, and appeared. The resurrection is a misdescription of survival.**

The reduction fails for specified reasons.

First, **crucifixion is a death-penalty designed to kill**. The narratives include verification: the centurion's confirmation to a surprised Pilate (Mark 15:44–45); the spear and the claim of sight (John 19:33–35); the release of the body only after that confirmation. A swoon-theory must convict the executioners of incompetence in their ordinary trade, and the prefect of releasing a condemned royal pretender still alive.

Second, **burial in a rock-tomb with a stone, spices, and, in John, bound graveclothes, is not a convalescent ward**. A man flogged and crucified, without modern medicine, who then moves the stone from inside, walks, and presents himself as the raised Lord, is a larger marvel than the claim the reduction meant to avoid. The reduction does not decrease miracle. It relocates it into physiology.

Third, **the apostolic claim is not resuscitation**. Romans 6:9: "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more." The appearances include wounds as marks of a death accomplished, not as injuries of a patient. A swooning Jesus would be a badly injured man in need of aid. The narratives present One who commissions, whose body is not under death's dominion, who is later proclaimed as exalted. The categories do not match.

Fourth, **the earliest formula says died, buried, raised**. A swoon is not a death, and a crawl from a tomb is not a raising by God as firstfruits. The reduction again changes the object.

Fifth, **a public ministry of a surviving, wounded pretender in Judea or Galilee would be a political fact of the same dangerous kind as the ministry that produced the cross**. The record is not of a hidden convalescence and a quiet retirement. It is of appearances, a commission, and then preaching of a raising by men who would be refuted by the living, recovering teacher if he were only that.

Some persons, in the world's ordinary course, have been taken down from punishment alive. That fact does not become a solvent of this execution, this verification, this burial, this proclamation, and this distinction from ministry-resuscitations. The swoon fails the penalty, the tomb, the claim's meaning, and the public aftermath.

The reduction fails.

---

# 46.38 Reason Through the Evidence

The reasoning may now be stated so that it can be inspected.

**Step 1.** The biblical writings are warranted as authentic written testimony of the claims under investigation (Movement V). The Person exists in first-century history and was crucified under Pontius Pilate (Chapter 43). He is identified as the Truth and the decisive revealer of the Father (Chapter 44). His public claims and works constitute a central authentication axis (Chapter 45). Those are earned premises.

**Step 2.** A death by crucifixion is a public execution. A burial is the disposal of a corpse in a place. A resurrection, in this testimony, is God's bodily raising of that buried man on the third day, attested by appearances. These are historical claims, not moods.

**Step 3.** Crucifixion under Pilate is historically secured as the public end of the ministry: Pauline scandal, fourfold passion, Acts-preaching at the scene, Tacitus, Josephus, an inscribed prefect, a window in the early 30s. The career of Chapter 45 runs toward this death as its legal and political crisis.

**Step 4.** Burial belongs to the earliest formula and to all four Gospel passion-closes. It is a named, placed, witnessed disposal, not optional decoration. The resurrection claim is a claim about this buried man.

**Step 5.** The resurrection claim, as specified, is bodily, public, and a claim of appearances. 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 is the earliest surviving apostolic form: received, delivered as gospel, sequential, named, checkable in the 50s, originating in the first years after the crucifixion. 1 Corinthians 15:12–19 ranks the raising as the hinge of preaching and faith.

**Step 6.** The Gospel passion and Easter narratives are later written testimony of the same sequential claim, distinguished by narrative detail — tomb-scene, women, Jerusalem and Galilee encounters, bodily marks — without being a different religion. Acts presents the public preaching as death-and-resurrection testimony.

**Step 7.** The witnesses themselves treat this conjunction as decisive: gospel-content, condition of their truthfulness, apostolic qualification, public witness, confession, hope. A crucified Messiah required this hinge if the claims of the career were not to end as refuted.

**Step 8.** The live reductions — spiritual survival, legend as global explanation, hallucination as global explanation, stolen body, swoon — fail as accounts of this conjunction. They explain a strand and cancel the structure.

**Step 9.** Therefore the investigator is warranted, with full force, in concluding that the authentic testimony presents the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ as the central historical claims of the career's end and of the apostolic message, that the death is historically secured as that end, that the resurrection claim is the early, bodily, public, appearance-claim of the same testimony, and that this presentation is the next established operation of Movement VI.

The form of reasoning is the same form the book has used: abductive historical and textual warrant. The writings say this. They are authentic testimony. The Person exists, has been identified, and has been authenticated in the ministry. The death is over-determined as public fact. The resurrection claim is early, structured, and ranked as hinge. The reductions fail. The central claims follow. It is not Euclidean demonstration. It is not impression. It is the exhibited bearing of the record upon the proposition.

---

# 46.39 Explicit Versus Inferred

The distinction is mandatory.

**Explicit in the biblical record:**

- "We preach Christ crucified" (1 Corinthians 1:23). "Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2).
- "Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: and that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve" — then five hundred, James, all the apostles, Paul (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).
- "If Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins." "We are found false witnesses of God" (1 Corinthians 15:15, 17).
- Crucifixion under Pilate, the inscription of kingship, Joseph's burial, the women's marking of the place, emptiness on the first day of the week, "he is risen; he is not here" (Mark 15–16 and parallels).
- "A spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have." The eating of fish (Luke 24:39–43).
- The wounds offered to Thomas (John 20:27).
- "This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses" (Acts 2:32). Acts 2:22–36; 3:15; 4:33; 10:40–41; 13:28–31; 17:31; 26:22–23.
- "Declared to be the Son of God with power … by the resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4).
- "If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved" (Romans 10:9).
- "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more" (Romans 6:9).
- "Witness … of his resurrection" as qualification (Acts 1:22).
- Predictions of suffering, death, and rising (Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34 and parallels).
- Matthew's record of the stolen-body rumour (Matthew 28:11–15).
- "I am the resurrection, and the life" (John 11:25). "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

**Inferred, and marked as inferred:**

- That "central historical claims" and "hinge" are accurate conceptual names for the ranking 1 Corinthians 15:1–19 and the Acts sermons exhibit. The phrases are the chapter's. The ranking is the record's.
- That the formula of 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 originated in the first years after the crucifixion rather than in the 50s. Reception-language, founding-delivery, and overlap with Cephas and James warrant the inference. The exact hour of first recitation is not recovered.
- That formula and Gospel narratives are two strata of one claim. The record does not itself print that comparative sentence. The comparison is an inference from overlapping sequence plus difference of literary form.
- That, given Movement V's warrant and Chapters 43–45, the investigator is entitled to treat these claims as the authentic testimony concerning the historical Person's end, not as late folklore. That entitlement is an inference from prior chapters plus the contents now examined.
- That the reductions fail as global explanations. Failure of a rival is an inferential conclusion from mismatch with the specified clauses, dates, names, bodily marks, and argumentative ranking.

**Not inferred here, because reserved:**

- That the dedicated eyewitness file is closed, including the full credibility-analysis of 2 Peter 1:16 (Chapter 47).
- That He confirms Scripture as Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 48). "According to the scriptures" is recorded as the formula's clause, not as that later case.
- That apostolic testimony carries His authority as a finished argument (Chapters 49–50).
- That the Graphē is primary written authority; that Scripture cannot be broken; that "thy word is truth" is the finished Graphē-gate (Movement VIII).
- Canon; infallibility; the Six First Principles; σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704).

The reader can therefore see which sentences are the Bible's and which are the chapter's reasoning from the Bible. The warranted conclusion in the next section is drawn from the explicit claims plus the marked inferences, not from the reserved files.

---

# 46.40 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The investigator is rationally warranted, with full force, in holding that:

> **Jesus Christ, the historical Person already established, already identified as the Truth and the revealer of the Father, and already presented as one whose public claims and works constitute a central authentication axis, was crucified under Pontius Pilate as the public end of that ministry, was buried, and is proclaimed from the earliest apostolic gospel-formula as having been raised on the third day and seen by named persons and groups. The death is a historically secured public execution, the crisis of the claims, not a private interior event. Burial belongs to the claim as a fact of the ordinary world. The resurrection claim is bodily, public, and a claim of appearances. 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 is the earliest surviving apostolic form of that claim: received, delivered as of first importance, checkable in the 50s, originating in the first years after the crucifixion. The Gospel passion and Easter narratives are later written testimony of the same sequential claim. The witnesses themselves treat death-and-resurrection as the hinge of their preaching, their truthfulness, their office, their confession, and their hope. The live reductions fail. This is the authentic testimony's positive case concerning the central historical claims of the career's end and their significance for apostolic testimony.**

The conclusion is not a passion-harmony of every hour. It is not a later council's vocabulary imposed backward. It is the career's end as the formula, the Gospels, and the Jerusalem sermon present it, now examined in its clauses and its ranking, attached to a man who occupied the reign of Tiberius, and warranted as the content of authentic testimony.

The conclusion is not hostage to Chapter 47. Eyewitnesses will be examined as a dedicated file. The appearances are already the claim's appointed attestation, and the ranking is already the witnesses' own. Later light is light on an object in hand. It is not the delayed arrival of the object.

A mere martyr has not been established as the ceiling of the file. A mere surviving influence has not been established as the ceiling of the file. The ceiling the record names is the conjunction: the One who is the Truth, crucified under Pilate, buried, raised on the third day, seen — the hinge on which apostolic testimony says it stands.

That is the verdict of this chapter. It is full force for this stage.

---

# 46.41 The Scope of This Stage

This is the scope statement for the death-and-resurrection claims. It is sequence and limitation of level, not a withdrawal of force.

By sequence, later chapters examine:

- the eyewitness testimony, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony (Chapter 47);
- Christ's confirmation of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to (Chapter 48);
- Christ's relationship to the apostles and the authority of their testimony (Chapters 49–50);
- the scriptural corpus, canonical recognition, and infallibility (Movement VII);
- John 10:34–36, "the scripture cannot be broken," "Thy word is truth" as Graphē-doctrine, and why the Graphē is the primary written authority (Movement VIII);
- mishandling, tergiversation, and ἄπειρος (*apeiros*, G552) (Movement IX);
- the scholarly labour of the Graphē, including σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704), and readiness for the Six First Principles (Movement X).

Those questions remain later because they are different questions. The present conclusion is already in force for its level.

This chapter has not treated the eyewitness file as complete. It has not established His confirmation of Scripture as a doctrine of the Graphē. It has not established apostolic authority as a finished argument. It has not claimed that the Graphē is primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. It has not treated John 10:34–36 as finished. It has not entered the First Principles. It has used "according to the scriptures" as the formula's own clause and left the Graphē-argument in its place. It has named seers as belonging to the claim and left their dedicated credibility-file in its place.

It has established that the authentic testimony presents the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ as the central historical claims of Movement VI at this stage, that the death is historically secured as the public end of the ministry, that the resurrection claim is the early bodily public appearance-claim of the same testimony, and that the witnesses themselves treat this conjunction as decisive.

Local questions of how a particular Easter scene was remembered, of the longer ending of Mark, of the guard-story's precise history, and of the exact year-date of Paul's reception of the formula remain as local questions. They are not a global rival. They do not reopen the death. They do not convert the four-clause claim into a maybe. They do not restore spiritual survival, legend, hallucination, theft, or swoon as adequate accounts of the conjunction.

One scope statement is enough. The force of the central claims is not diminished by the existence of later chapters.

---

# 46.42 Apply the Standard

The reader should now be able to take any proposed sentence about "Easter" or "the death of Jesus" and ask:

> **Is this sentence a claim of historical existence, a claim of identity with the Truth, a claims-and-works authentication, a death-and-resurrection claim, or a reserved file of eyewitness, Scripture-confirmation, or apostolic authority?**

Then:

> **If it is a death-and-resurrection sentence, which clause is it — died, buried, raised, seen — in what source-form, formula or narrative, and does the proposed account keep the sequence?**

Then:

> **Does the proposed reduction explain 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, 1 Corinthians 15:12–19, Mark 15–16:8, Luke 24:36–43, John 20:27, Acts 2:22–32, and Romans 1:4 together, or only a preferred strand?**

Then:

> **Is the conclusion being postponed because later chapters remain, or is it being drawn at the level the grounds support?**

If the grounds are the authentic testimony's explicit death, burial, raising, and appearances, attached to the historical Person already identified as the Truth and already authenticated in the ministry, with the death independently over-determined and the reductions failing, the central claims are to be granted with full force.

If a later conclusion is desired — that the eyewitnesses of His majesty are a closed file, that He confirms Scripture, that apostolic testimony carries His authority — it is to be sought in its chapter, not smuggled into this hinge and not used to postpone this hinge.

If a catalogue of "resurrection proofs" mixes Tacitus' sentence with later pious legend and with the virtue of the churches, the catalogue is to be classified before it is allowed to speak of these claims. Tacitus can warrant a death under Pilate. He cannot narrate Easter. Classification is the discipline of the whole book.

The governing maxim remains:

> **Do not make the reader choose between reason and Scripture. Teach the reader to reason through Scripture.**

Reasoning through the writings at this stage, concerning the Person already located, identified, and authenticated in the ministry, yields death and resurrection as the central historical claims of Movement VI. That is not the abandonment of historical method. It is the refusal to separate what the record joins, and the refusal to call that joining a postponement.

---

# 46.43 From Death and Resurrection to Eyewitness Testimony

A claim of appearances is already a claim of witnesses. The formula names them. The Gospels narrate them. Acts makes witness of the resurrection a qualification of office. 1 Corinthians 15:15 makes their truthfulness hang upon the event.

That is not yet the dedicated eyewitness file.

The next necessary question is not a new curiosity. It is the question the hinge itself creates. If the central historical claims are death, burial, raising, and seeing, then the seeing must be examined as testimony: who saw, what constitutes an eyewitness of these things, what 2 Peter 1:16 means by being eyewitnesses of His majesty, how proximity, knowledge, consistency, and credibility function when the object is this Person's glory and this Person's raising.

Chapter 18 established witness as a category. Chapter 35 established credibility-conditions. Chapter 47 must apply those instruments to the testimony concerning Christ as the assignment of Movement VI, not as a general lecture on witnesses repeated.

The question is therefore not:

> **Are death and resurrection the central historical claims of the career's end, and do the witnesses themselves treat them as the hinge?**

That question has been answered.

The question is:

> **What is the eyewitness testimony concerning this Person, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony, and what does that testimony establish as a dedicated file now that the object of sight includes both the ministry's majesty and the raising?**

That question is not a retreat from the hinge. It is the hinge's appointed attestation examined as attestation. A raising without witnesses is not this gospel. Witnesses without a dedicated examination of their seeing would leave Movement VI's central claims named and their seers unexamined. The investigation therefore moves from:

> **He was crucified, buried, and — the testimony claims, early, bodily, publicly — raised and seen.**

to:

> **Who are the eyewitnesses, and what does their testimony, as testimony, warrant?**

That is the proper open of the next chapter of Movement VI. The hinge was never meant to be the last word. It was meant to be a word sufficient to justify taking the next one, which is the word the apostles themselves placed next: "whereof we are witnesses."

---

# What Has Been Established

This chapter has established:

1. **The question of the death and resurrection of Christ is the question of the public end of the authenticated career and of the claimed bodily reversal of that end, asked of the historical Person already established, with the witnesses' own ranking of these claims as part of the object.**
2. **Historical existence, revelatory identity, claims-and-works authentication, death-and-resurrection as central historical claims, the dedicated eyewitness file, and Scripture-confirmation / apostolic-authority files are six distinct objects.**
3. **Death, in this chapter, is the public crucifixion of Jesus under Pontius Pilate, the historically secured termination of the earthly ministry.**
4. **Burial is the claimed interment of the crucified body in a known tomb, a belonging fact in the earliest sequence, not optional decoration.**
5. **Resurrection is the claim that God raised this buried man bodily on the third day and that He was seen. It is not spiritual survival, legend as such, ministry-raising of another, or apotheosis.**
6. **Crucifixion under Pilate is the public, legally and geographically located end of the Chapter 45 career, among the most secure facts in the file, the crisis of the claims.**
7. **The death is not a private interior event. Particulars, verification, titulus, and hostile Roman memory locate it in the world.**
8. **The passion sequence in all four Gospels, and the pre-Pauline formula, make the same man die a public death at Jerusalem and make burial the next fact.**
9. **The Jewish charge concerns the claim; the Roman charge concerns kingship. The inscription is the career's last public sentence before Easter.**
10. **Burial is coordinated with death and raising in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4. Remove it and the claim changes.**
11. **Joseph of Arimathea, a known rock-tomb, and the women as markers of the place narrate the burial-clause as a local, checkable disposal.**
12. **The resurrection proposition has a subject (this Jesus), a predicate (bodily raising), a time-marker (the third day), and a mode of attestation (appearances).**
13. **The claim is bodily: Luke 24:39, John 20:27, 1 Corinthians 15:44 as σῶμα, Acts 2:31 on flesh not seeing corruption. Mere spiritual survival is a different claim.**
14. **The claim is public: Jerusalem preaching, a tomb-dispute, living named witnesses in the 50s. A private interior vision is not the whole claim.**
15. **Appearances are structured: Cephas, the twelve, five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, Paul. The mix of seers is part of the claim.**
16. **The third day and the empty tomb belong to the claim. Distinction of formula and narrative is not dismissal of either.**
17. **1 Corinthians 15:3–8, in letter-context, is the earliest surviving apostolic form: received, delivered as gospel, sequential, named, checkable.**
18. **The formula is older than the letter: founding-delivery, reception after conversion, overlap with Cephas and James, a pre-Pauline movement he persecuted.**
19. **The four clauses — died, buried, raised, seen — are not optional metaphors. Remove any and the remaining religion is not this gospel.**
20. **Named recipients make the formula checkable in the 50s. "The greater part remain" is an invitation to inquiry.**
21. **1 Corinthians 15:12–19 states the hinge: if Christ is not raised, preaching, faith, witness-truthfulness, forgiveness as preached, and hope for the dead collapse.**
22. **The Gospel narratives are later written testimony of the same sequential claim. Difference of date is not a license to dismiss the narratives.**
23. **Early formula and later narrative detail are two strata of one claim. Neither flattening nor playing them against each other is warranted.**
24. **Empty-tomb narratives have a common structure, women as first discoverers, and emptiness as a public-world claim. They are not to be dismissed because Paul lists official seers rather than a morning's discovery.**
25. **Appearance-narratives locate Jerusalem and Galilee, name persons, insist on bodily marks and table-fellowship, join the event to the Scriptures, and send witnesses.**
26. **Acts presents apostolic preaching as death-and-resurrection testimony from Jerusalem to Athens. Acts 1:22 ranks witness of the resurrection as qualification.**
27. **Significance for apostolic testimony is the record's own ranking: gospel-content, truthfulness, office, public power, confession (Romans 10:9), hope.**
28. **A crucified Messiah required this hinge if the career's claims were not to end as refuted. Predictions come due. Acts 2:22–24 is the grammar: approved, crucified, raised.**
29. **Spiritual survival, legendary accretion, hallucination as global explanation, stolen body, and swoon fail as accounts of the conjunction.**
30. **This examination does not circularly assume Movement VIII. Movement V warrants the writings as testimony. Chapters 43–45 locate, identify, and authenticate the Person in the ministry. This chapter examines the career's end.**
31. **The investigator is rationally warranted, with full force, in treating death and resurrection as the central historical claims of Movement VI in the sense this chapter has defined.**
32. **What is reserved is Chapters 47–50 in full; canon; infallibility; John 10 / "cannot be broken"; John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine; First Principles; *spoudazō*; and the Graphē as primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense.**

---

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter's central conclusion:** Jesus Christ, already established as a historical figure of the early first century, already identified as the Truth and the revealer of the Father, and already presented as one whose claims and works constitute a public authentication axis, was crucified under Pontius Pilate as the public end of that ministry, was buried, and is proclaimed from the earliest apostolic formula as raised on the third day and seen. The death is historically secured. Burial belongs. The resurrection claim is bodily, public, and a claim of appearances. 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 is the earliest form; the Gospels are later written testimony of the same claim. The witnesses themselves treat this conjunction as the hinge. The reductions fail. The central claims are full force for this stage. The investigation now turns to the eyewitness testimony.

The essential architecture is:

> **Authenticated career → death as public end → burial as belonging fact → resurrection specified → earliest formula → later narratives of the same claim → hinge of apostolic testimony → failure of reductions → central claims warranted → sequence to the eyewitness file.**

The governing distinctions are:

- **Existence** is Chapter 43's object; **identity with truth** is Chapter 44's object; **claims-and-works** is Chapter 45's object; **death-and-resurrection** is this chapter's object.
- **Death** is not a private interior event.
- **Burial** is not optional decoration.
- **Resurrection** is not spiritual survival, legend, hallucination, theft, or swoon.
- **Early formula** is not **later narrative**, and neither is a rival gospel.
- **Naming seers** is not **closing the eyewitness file**.
- **"According to the scriptures"** is not **Christ's confirmation of Scripture as Graphē-doctrine**.
- **Scope** is sequence of levels, not hesitation about this level.

The decisive principle is:

> **Examine the public end of the authenticated career and the claimed bodily reversal before treating the dedicated eyewitness file or drawing the Graphē-gate. Draw the conclusion the premises support. Do not draw the conclusions that still require later premises. Then ask what the eyewitness testimony establishes.**

---

# Transition to Chapter 47

Movement VI continues.

The central witness has been located in history. He has been identified as the Truth and the revealer of the Father. His public claims and public works have been examined as a single authentication axis. His death under Pontius Pilate has now been taken as the public, historically secured end of that ministry, His burial as a belonging fact, and His resurrection as the early, bodily, public, appearance-claim of the same authentic testimony — the hinge the witnesses themselves treat as decisive.

The writings that present that hinge do not leave the seeing unnamed. They name Cephas, the twelve, five hundred, James, the apostles, Paul, the women, the gathered disciples. They record Peter saying that they had not followed cunningly devised fables but were eyewitnesses of His majesty. They make witness of the resurrection a qualification of office. The next necessary question is therefore not a new curiosity. It is the appointed attestation of the hinge, examined as testimony:

> **What is the eyewitness testimony concerning Jesus Christ, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony, and what does that testimony establish now that the object of sight is this Person's ministry and this Person's raising?**

That is the subject of:

# Chapter 47 — The Eyewitness Testimony

> **Examine eyewitness evidence, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony.**

The investigation now moves from:

> **the death and resurrection**
>
> to:
>
> **the eyewitness testimony.**

# End of Chapter 46

title: The Eyewitness Testimony
body:
> **Movement VI — Christ as the Central Witness**

> **Central objective:** Examine eyewitness evidence, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony. Show, with full force and from the authentic testimony now attached to a historical Person already identified as the Truth, whose public claims and works already function as an authentication axis, and whose death and resurrection already stand as the central historical claims of the career's end, that eyewitness testimony in this argument is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard — not mere presence and not later commentary; that 2 Peter 1:16–18 grounds that category explicitly in the Transfiguration; that the resurrection appearances are claimed eyewitness events of the risen Christ; that other positioned witnesses of the public ministry belong with proportional force; and that this testimony is a central authentication line of Movement VI at the level earned so far.

---

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 46 established that the historical Person of Chapter 43, already identified in Chapter 44 as the Truth and the decisive revealer of the Father, and already presented in Chapter 45 as one whose public claims and public works belong together as a central authentication axis, was crucified under Pontius Pilate as the public, historically secured end of that ministry, was buried, and is proclaimed from the earliest apostolic formula as having been raised on the third day and seen by named persons and groups. Death-and-resurrection is the hinge the witnesses themselves treat as decisive. That hinge is already in force.

Chapter 46 ended by naming the next necessary question, not a new curiosity:

> **What is the eyewitness testimony concerning this Person, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony, and what does that testimony establish now that the object of sight is this Person's ministry and this Person's raising?**

That is this chapter's assignment.

The locked Table of Contents states the work in one sentence:

> **Examine eyewitness evidence, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony.**

The chapter does not re-prove historical existence. It cites Chapter 43 as established. It does not re-argue identity with the Truth. It cites Chapter 44 as established. It does not re-try the claims-and-works conjunction. It cites Chapter 45 as established. It does not re-try the death-and-resurrection case. It cites Chapter 46 as established. It does not treat Christ's confirmation of Scripture as Graphē-doctrine. It does not treat apostolic authority as a finished argument of office. It does not consummate canon, infallibility, or the Graphē as primary written authority. It performs the examination without which those later investigations would be investigations of a named identity whose career had been authenticated, whose end had been examined as hinge, and whose seers had then been left unnamed as a file.

A claim of appearances is already a claim of witnesses. The formula names them. The Gospels narrate them. Acts makes witness of the resurrection a qualification of office. 2 Peter 1:16 states the category in the first person: they were not followers of cunningly devised fables but eyewitnesses of His majesty. Naming seers as belonging to the hinge was Chapter 46's right. Examining their seeing as testimony is this chapter's work.

The remaining questions of Movement VI follow by sequence. Sequence continues the investigation. It does not convert the present line into hesitation.

---

## Central Objective

> **To define eyewitness testimony, in this argument, as positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard; to distinguish that object from mere presence, from later commentary, from testimony in general, from apostolic office as a finished doctrine, and from Christ's confirmation of Scripture; to examine 2 Peter 1:16–18 in context as an explicit biblical grounding of the category; to treat the resurrection appearances as claimed eyewitness events of the risen Christ without re-trying Chapter 46; to give other positioned witnesses of the public ministry their proportional force; to expose the reductions that fail; and to state, with full force, that eyewitness testimony is a central authentication line of Movement VI in the sense this chapter defines.**

The governing movement is:

> **Hinge already in force → question of the seers → definition of eyewitness as positioned knowledge → distinctions that protect the object → 2 Peter 1:16–18 as explicit grounding → Transfiguration as the named event → related apostolic testimony of seeing and hearing → resurrection appearances as eyewitness events → positioned witnesses of the ministry → failure of reductions → inspectable inference → warranted authentication line → sequence to Christ's confirmation of Scripture.**

The chapter's conclusion is affirmative:

> **Eyewitness testimony, in this argument, is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard. It is not mere presence in a crowd, and it is not later commentary upon an event. 2 Peter 1:16–18 grounds that category explicitly: the proclamation of the Lord's power and coming is set over against cunningly devised fables by the claim that the speakers were eyewitnesses of His majesty, having received honour and glory from the Father, having heard the voice from heaven, having been with Him in the holy mount. The Transfiguration is the named event of that claim. The resurrection appearances, already established in Chapter 46 as the appointed attestation of the raising, are here examined as claimed eyewitness events of the risen Christ. Other positioned witnesses of the public ministry — the disciples who companied with Him, the women as markers of the tomb and first reporters of emptiness, the named lists that make inquiry possible — belong with proportional force. Eyewitness is not all testimony. Apostolic eyewitness is not yet the finished doctrine of apostolic office. Seeing and hearing is not yet Christ's confirmation of Scripture. The authentic testimony's positive case is that this Person was seen and heard by positioned witnesses of His ministry's majesty and of His raising. That case is a central authentication line of Movement VI, stated here with full force. It is not yet His confirmation of the Graphē, nor the later doctrine of the Graphē as primary written authority.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The authentication line is already in force.

# 47.1 The Question Created by the Preceding Chapter

Movement VI has located a Person, identified Him as the Truth, examined His public claims and works as an authentication axis, and taken His death and resurrection as the central historical claims of the career's end. It has not yet examined the seeing by which those claims are attested as testimony.

Chapter 43 established existence, publicity, chronology, Jewish setting, crucifixion under Pilate, and the failure of myth and coreless legend. Chapter 44 established identity with the Truth and decisive revelation of the Father. Chapter 45 established the claims-and-works conjunction as a central authentication axis. Chapter 46 established crucifixion as the public end of that ministry, burial as a belonging fact, and resurrection as the early, bodily, public, appearance-claim of the same testimony — the hinge the witnesses themselves treat as decisive. Those conclusions are premises here.

A Person can be located, identified, authenticated in the ministry, and examined at the hinge of death and raising, and a further question still remains: who saw, and what kind of knowledge is the seeing they claim? Identity that is never encountered is not the identity the Gospels present. A hinge that is never attested by seers is not the hinge 1 Corinthians 15 presents. The writings that have now been used as authentic testimony do not stop at the clauses "died, buried, raised." They add "he was seen." They record Peter saying that they were eyewitnesses of His majesty. They make witness of the resurrection a qualification of the one who would take Judas's place. Those are further claims about the same career. They are the claims for which a historical baseline, a revelatory identification, an authentication axis, and a hinge of death and raising now exist.

The question is therefore not:

> **Did a man named Jesus occupy Galilee and Judea under Tiberius, is He presented as the Truth, do His claims and works function as an authentication axis, and are death and resurrection the central historical claims of the career's end?**

Those questions have been answered.

The question is:

> **What is the eyewitness testimony concerning this Person, and what does that testimony, as testimony, warrant now that the object of sight includes both the ministry's majesty and the raising?**

If presence stood alone, Movement VI would be the investigation of crowds. If later commentary stood alone, Movement VI would be the investigation of sermons about an unseen past. If eyewitness testimony is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard, Movement VI is the investigation of seers attached to the One who is the Truth.

That is a different operation from piety. It is the operation this chapter must perform.

# 47.2 What This Chapter Does Not Repeat

Chapter 18 established witness as an evidential category: eyewitness, participant-witness, apostolic witness, investigative witness, received testimony, and Christ as the faithful witness. It named 2 Peter 1:16, Luke 1:1–4, 1 John 1:1–3, and 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 as belonging to that architecture. It did not try the Movement VI file of the seers of this Person.

Chapter 27 established the apostolic office as a mode of giving. It did not close the authority of apostolic testimony as Movement VI's later assignment, and it does not close it here.

Chapter 34 established testimony as a legitimate form of historical evidence, always related to a particular proposition.

Chapter 35 established credibility-conditions: opportunity to know, proximity, observation distinguished from interpretation, sincerity distinguished from accuracy, consistency, independence, corroboration, named witnesses, unfavorable testimony, and the distinction between witness-writer, witness-source-writer, and tradition-writer. It noted 2 Peter 1:16–18, 1 John 1:1–3, Luke 1:1–4, and 1 Corinthians 15 as exhibiting those conditions. It reserved the dedicated application of those instruments to Christ as the assignment of Movement VI.

Chapter 42 established the warrant to treat the biblical writings as authentic written testimony of the claims under investigation, and used 2 Peter 1:16–21 as a warrant-form: denial of fable, eyewitness of majesty, prophetic word, the charge to take heed. It reserved the filling of that form as Movement VI's work.

Chapter 43 established the historical Person. Chapter 44 established identity with the Truth. Chapter 45 established the claims-and-works conjunction. It does not treat "according to the scriptures" as the finished doctrine that He confirms the Graphē. It does not treat Acts 1:22 as the finished argument of apostolic office. The new function is this:

> **To isolate the eyewitness testimony concerning the historical Person as the next necessary question about the One already identified as the Truth, already authenticated in the ministry, and already examined at the hinge of death and raising, using the writings as the authentic testimony of what was seen and heard, and to state what that testimony warrants before Movement VI develops His confirmation of Scripture and the authority of the apostolic witness.**

# 47.3 Define the Question: Eyewitness Testimony as Positioned Knowledge

An **eyewitness**, in this chapter, is a person whose knowledge of an event is knowledge of what that person saw and heard from a position that made such knowledge possible.

**Eyewitness testimony**, in this argument, is the communication of that knowledge. It is not the mere fact that a body occupied a space near an event. It is not a later homily, commentary, or reconstruction offered by someone who was not so positioned. It is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard, given as testimony.

Three marks belong to the definition.

First, **position**. The witness occupied a place and a time from which the event could be known. Position is geographical, temporal, and personal. Peter, James, and John on the mountain were positioned for the Transfiguration. Mary Magdalene at the tomb on the first day of the week was positioned for the discovery of emptiness. Paul on the Damascus road was positioned for the appearance he claims. A later reader of their writings is not so positioned. The later reader receives testimony.

Second, **knowledge**. Position without knowledge is not eyewitness. A man may stand in a crowd at a crucifixion and know only that a condemned person died. Another may stand nearer, hear the inscription, see the women, and know specified facts. Eyewitness is knowledge, not occupancy. The biblical language is the language of seeing, hearing, beholding, handling, and then bearing witness — a movement from encounter to knowledge to speech.

Third, **what was seen and heard**. The object is sensory encounter of a specified event, not later interpretation detached from that encounter. Interpretation may follow. Chapter 35 already distinguished observation from interpretation. This chapter takes that distinction as a premise. The eyewitness claim is a claim about the encounter. Later commentary may be true, false, or mixed. It is a different kind of speech.

**Central authentication line**, in this chapter, names the function of that testimony inside Movement VI. The locked TOC assigns this chapter eyewitness evidence, including 2 Peter 1:16 and related apostolic testimony. The assignment is therefore not a free selection of pious scenes of seeing. It is the examination of what the record places as the human link between the authenticated Person and later knowledge of Him.

The question of this chapter joins those definitions:

> **Does the authentic testimony present positioned witnesses of what was seen and heard concerning this Person — of His majesty in the ministry and of His raising — such that their testimony functions as a central authentication line of Movement VI?**

Several elements belong to the question as this chapter defines it.

First, **explicit biblical grounding**. 2 Peter 1:16–18 does not merely illustrate a modern category. It names the category: eyewitnesses of His majesty, over against fables, with seeing and hearing specified, and with the holy mount as the place.

Second, **the resurrection appearances as eyewitness events**. Chapter 46 established that "he was seen" belongs to the hinge. This chapter examines that seeing as testimony: who was positioned, what they claim to have seen, how the claim is given.

Third, **other positioned witnesses of the public ministry**, given proportional force: disciples who companied with Him from John's baptism, women who marked the tomb and first reported emptiness, named lists that make inquiry possible.

Fourth, **examinability**. These are claims inside a warranted written testimony about a historical Person. They can be defined, distinguished, compared with reductions, and reasoned through. They are not exempt from investigation because they are theological. They are not reduced to psychology because they are personal.

Thus:

> **The question of the eyewitness testimony is the question of positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard concerning the historical Person already established, under the writings already warranted as testimony, with 2 Peter 1:16–18 as an explicit grounding of the category and with the resurrection appearances as claimed eyewitness events of the raising.**

# 47.4 Distinguish Six Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats six different objects as one.

## 47.4.1 Historical existence, identity, claims-and-works, and the hinge

These are the objects of Chapters 43–46. They include a real person, identity with the Truth, the public authentication axis of claims and works, and death-and-resurrection as the central historical claims of the career's end. Those conclusions are premises here. This chapter does not re-try them. It examines the seers of the Person so established.

## 47.4.2 Eyewitness testimony as positioned knowledge

This is the object of the present chapter. It includes: the definition of eyewitness as positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard; 2 Peter 1:16–18 in context as explicit grounding; the Transfiguration as the named event of that claim; the resurrection appearances as claimed eyewitness events; other positioned witnesses of the public ministry with proportional force; the failure of specified reductions; and the warrant for treating this testimony as a central authentication line of Movement VI.

## 47.4.3 Testimony in general

Not all testimony is eyewitness testimony. Chapter 18 already distinguished direct eyewitness, participant-witness, investigative witness, documentary or transmitted witness, prophetic witness, and revelatory witness. Luke investigates what eyewitnesses delivered. Paul receives and delivers a formula he also confirms by his own seeing. A prophet bears witness of what he received. Those are real forms of testimony. They are not this chapter's defined object. Collapsing them into "eyewitness" inflates the word until it means every speaker. Restricting "testimony" to eyewitness starves the record of forms it actually uses. The distinction protects both.

## 47.4.4 Mere presence

A crowd is not a panel of eyewitnesses. Presence is a necessary condition of ordinary seeing. It is not a sufficient condition of positioned knowledge. The Gospels themselves distinguish the many who saw signs from the few who are named as witnesses of specified events. Acts 10:41 distinguishes showing Him openly from showing Him to all the people. Presence without knowledge, or presence without specified encounter, is not the object under examination.

## 47.4.5 Later commentary

A later writer may speak truly about an event he did not see. He may also speak falsely. In either case his speech is not eyewitness testimony. Homily, theology, liturgy, and reconstruction are further operations. They may rest upon eyewitness testimony. They are not substitutes for it. The investigator who treats a second-century interpretation of the Transfiguration as if it were Peter's "we were with him in the holy mount" has changed the object.

## 47.4.6 Confirmation of Scripture and apostolic authority as office

Chapter 48 examines Christ's treatment of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative. Chapters 49–50 examine His relationship to the apostles and the authority of their testimony. Seeing the Transfiguration is not yet His confirmation of the Graphē. Being an eyewitness of the resurrection is a qualification named in Acts 1:22; it is not yet the finished doctrine that apostolic testimony carries His authority as a closed case of office. Those files remain later because they are different questions.

The governing distinction is therefore:

> **Prior Movement VI conclusions ≠ eyewitness as positioned knowledge ≠ testimony in general ≠ mere presence ≠ later commentary ≠ Scripture-confirmation and apostolic-office files.**

Each is a real object. Each has its place. This chapter takes the second.

# 47.6 Eyewitness Defined: Positioned Knowledge of What Was Seen and Heard

The definition may now be stated with the precision the argument requires.

An eyewitness is not "anyone who was nearby." An eyewitness is a person who, from a position that made knowledge possible, saw and heard a specified event, and whose testimony is the communication of that knowledge.

**Positioned** names the relation between the person and the event. The mountain, the tomb, the locked room, the lakeside, the Damascus road — these are not decorations. They are the places at which knowledge of this kind is claimed. Without position, "I saw" is an empty verb.

**Knowledge** names the cognitive content. The witness knows that this occurred, not merely that he occupied a space while something occurred. The biblical movement is from encounter to witness-speech: "that which we have seen and heard declare we unto you" (1 John 1:3). Declaration without prior seeing and hearing is a different speech. Seeing and hearing without declaration may be private. Testimony is the joining of the two.

**What was seen and heard** names the object as sensory encounter. The Transfiguration is seen majesty and heard voice. The appearances are seeing of the raised One, and in specified narratives hearing, touching, and eating. The tomb-morning is seeing of emptiness and hearing of announcement. These are not metaphors of insight. They are claims of encounter in the world.

The definition excludes two counterfeits at once.

It excludes the reduction of eyewitness to **mere presence**. Occupancy is not knowledge.

It excludes the inflation of eyewitness to **later commentary**. A true sentence about an unseen event is not an eyewitness sentence.

Thus:

> **Eyewitness testimony in this argument is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard, communicated as testimony. Presence without that knowledge is not the object. Later speech without that position is not the object.**

---

# 47.7 Presence Is Not Eyewitness

The distinction requires its own statement because the word "witness" is commonly stretched to cover everyone who was in the vicinity.

The Gospels themselves refuse the stretch. Crowds follow. Crowds eat bread. Crowds see signs. Crowds cry "Hosanna" and "Crucify." Those crowds are historically real. They are not, by that fact, the eyewitness file. John 6:26 records that many sought Him because they ate of the loaves and were filled, not because they saw signs as signs. Presence at a feeding is not positioned knowledge of what the feeding meant, and it is not even, in that sentence, positioned knowledge of the sign as sign.

Acts 10:40–41 is explicit about a further limit. God raised Him and "shewed him openly; not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before of God, even to us, who did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead." Open showing, not to all the people. The appearances are real encounters in the world. They are not a demonstration before Pilate's tribunal. The limitation is the record's description of the mode. Chosen witnesses, including table-fellowship after the raising, are the positioned class. The city that knew the crucifixion is not thereby a city of eyewitnesses of the raising.

The same distinction applies to the Transfiguration. Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2, and Luke 9:28 name three: Peter, James, and John. The rest of the Twelve are nearby in the narrative world and are not on the mountain. Presence in the company of Jesus is not presence on the holy mount. 2 Peter 1:18 says "when we were with him in the holy mount." The "we" is the positioned we, not the census of all disciples.

Presence remains relevant. It is the ordinary condition of seeing. Chapter 35 already made opportunity to know foundational to credibility. This chapter does not retract that. It refuses to treat opportunity as identical with testimony. Opportunity is a condition. Eyewitness is knowledge under that condition, given as speech.

Thus:

> **Mere presence is a condition of ordinary seeing. It is not eyewitness testimony. The record itself names specified seers of specified events and distinguishes them from the surrounding many.**

---

# 47.8 Later Commentary Is Not Eyewitness

The distinction requires its own statement because later speech about Christ is abundant, and some of it is true.

A commentary may correctly say that Jesus was transfigured. A liturgy may correctly confess that He rose from the dead. A historian may correctly conclude that the crucifixion occurred under Pilate. None of those sentences, as later sentences, is eyewitness testimony. They may rest upon eyewitness testimony. They may also rest upon other grounds. The kind of speech they are is not the kind 2 Peter 1:16 is.

2 Peter 1:16 is first-person and event-located: we were eyewitnesses; we heard this voice; we were with Him in the holy mount. 1 John 1:1–3 is first-person and sensory: we have heard, seen with our eyes, looked upon, handled.
