**Step 6.** Other positioned witnesses of the public ministry — disciples who companied from the beginning, Peter as continuous participant, John as sensory witness, Paul as later encounter-witness of a different proximity-class — belong to the file as specified, not as a flattened crowd.

**Step 7.** The live reductions — mere presence, later commentary as eyewitness, legend as global displacement, hallucination as global account of the seers, collusion as global fabrication — fail as accounts of this conjunction. They explain a strand and cancel the structure.

**Step 8.** Therefore the investigator is warranted, with full force, in concluding that the authentic testimony presents positioned witnesses of what was seen and heard concerning Jesus Christ — of His majesty in the ministry and of His raising — and that this presentation is a central authentication line of Movement VI, the next established operation after the hinge.

The form of reasoning is the same form the book has used: abductive historical and textual warrant. The writings say this. They are authentic testimony. The Person exists, has been identified, authenticated, and examined at the hinge. The seers are specified, mixed, named, and ranked by the record as witnesses of what they saw and heard. The reductions fail. The authentication line follows. It is not Euclidean demonstration. It is not impression. It is the exhibited bearing of the record upon the proposition.

---

# 47.43 Explicit Versus Inferred

The distinction is mandatory.

**Explicit in the biblical record:**

- "We have not followed cunningly devised fables ... but were eyewitnesses of his majesty." "This voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount" (2 Peter 1:16–18).
- Transfiguration narratives: Peter, James, and John; the mountain; glory; Moses and Elijah; the Father's voice (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36).
- "That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled" (1 John 1:1–3).
- "He that saw it bare record" (John 19:35). "This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true" (John 21:24).
- "We beheld his glory" (John 1:14).
- "Eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word" who delivered; Luke's orderly account for certainty (Luke 1:1–4).
- "Must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection" from those who companied from John's baptism (Acts 1:21–22).
- "This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses" (Acts 2:32). "We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20). Acts 3:15; 5:32; 10:39–41; 13:31.
- "Ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning" (John 15:27). "Ye are witnesses of these things" (Luke 24:48). "Ye shall be witnesses unto me" (Acts 1:8).
- "He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve" — five hundred, James, all the apostles, Paul (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). "Have I seen Jesus Christ our Lord?" (1 Corinthians 9:1). "We are found false witnesses of God" if He is not raised (1 Corinthians 15:15).
- Women mark the burial, come first on the first day, report, are not at first believed (Mark 15:47; 16:1–8; Luke 23:55–24:11; John 20:1–18).
- "A witness of the sufferings of Christ" (1 Peter 5:1).

**Inferred, and marked as inferred:**

- That "positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard" is an accurate conceptual name for the species 2 Peter 1:16–18, 1 John 1:1–3, Luke 1:2, and the Acts sermons exhibit. The phrase is the chapter's. The species is the record's.
- That 2 Peter 1:16–18 names the Transfiguration as narrated in the Synoptics. The letter names mount, voice, beloved Son, majesty. The identification is an inference from corresponding marks, not a verse that prints the word "transfiguration."
- That formula and Gospel appearance-narratives are two strata of one seeing-claim. Chapter 46 already marked the parallel inference for the hinge. This chapter extends it to the seers as seers.
- That, given Movement V's warrant and Chapters 43–46, the investigator is entitled to treat these seeing-claims as the authentic testimony concerning the historical Person's seers, not as late folklore. That entitlement is an inference from prior chapters plus the contents now examined.
- That the reductions fail as global explanations. Failure of a rival is an inferential conclusion from mismatch with the specified clauses, dates, names, mix of seers, and argumentative ranking.

**Not inferred here, because reserved:**

- That He confirms Scripture as Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 48). 2 Peter 1:19–21 is named as the letter's turn, not as that later case. Luke 24's opening of Moses and the prophets is recorded as belonging to an appearance, not as that later case.
- That apostolic testimony carries His authority as a finished argument of office (Chapters 49–50). Acts 1:22 is used as eyewitness-qualification, not as that later case.
- That the Graphē is primary written authority; that Scripture cannot be broken; that "thy word is truth" is the finished Graphē-gate (Movement VIII).
- Canon; infallibility; the Six First Principles; σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704).

The reader can therefore see which sentences are the Bible's and which are the chapter's reasoning from the Bible. The warranted conclusion in the next section is drawn from the explicit claims plus the marked inferences, not from the reserved files.

# 47.44 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The investigator is rationally warranted, with full force, in holding that:

> **Eyewitness testimony concerning Jesus Christ, in the authentic testimony now attached to the historical Person already established, identified, authenticated in the ministry, and examined at the hinge of death and raising, is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard. It is not mere presence, and it is not later commentary. 2 Peter 1:16–18 grounds the category explicitly: the speakers have not followed cunningly devised fables but were eyewitnesses of His majesty, having heard the Father's voice when they were with Him in the holy mount. The Transfiguration is that named event. The resurrection appearances are claimed eyewitness events of the risen Christ: ordered and named in 1 Corinthians 15:5–8, narrated as seeing in the Gospels, with women as markers of the place and first reporters of emptiness, and with named lists that make inquiry possible. Disciples of the public ministry, Peter as continuous participant, John as sensory witness, and Paul as later encounter-witness belong with specified, proportional force. The live reductions fail. This is the authentic testimony's positive case concerning the seers of this Person, and it is a central authentication line of Movement VI.**

The conclusion is not a harmony of every hour of seeing. It is not a later council's vocabulary imposed backward. It is the seers as the letter, the Gospels, the formula, and the Jerusalem sermons present them, now examined under a definition the record itself exhibits, attached to a man who occupied the reign of Tiberius, and warranted as the content of authentic testimony.

The conclusion is not hostage to Chapter 48. His confirmation of Scripture will be examined as a dedicated file. The seers are already the appointed human link between the authenticated Person and later knowledge of Him. Later light is light on an object in hand. It is not the delayed arrival of the object.

A mere crowd has not been established as the ceiling of the file. A mere later homily has not been established as the ceiling of the file. The ceiling the record names is positioned knowledge: we were eyewitnesses of His majesty; we have seen and heard; He was seen; we are witnesses.

That is the verdict of this chapter. It is full force for this stage.

# 47.45 The Scope of This Stage

This is the scope statement for the eyewitness line. It is sequence and limitation of level, not a withdrawal of force.

By sequence, later chapters examine:

- Christ's confirmation of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to (Chapter 48);
- Christ's relationship to the apostles and the authority of their testimony (Chapters 49–50);
- the scriptural corpus, canonical recognition, and infallibility (Movement VII);
- John 10:34–36, "the scripture cannot be broken," "Thy word is truth" as Graphē-doctrine, and why the Graphē is the primary written authority (Movement VIII);
- mishandling, tergiversation, and ἄπειρος (*apeiros*, G552) (Movement IX);
- the scholarly labour of the Graphē, including σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704), and readiness for the Six First Principles (Movement X).

Those questions remain later because they are different questions. The present conclusion is already in force for its level.

This chapter has not established His confirmation of Scripture as a doctrine of the Graphē. It has not established apostolic authority as a finished argument of office. It has not claimed that the Graphē is primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. It has not treated John 10:34–36 as finished. It has not entered the First Principles. It has used 2 Peter 1:16–18 as the eyewitness unit and left 1:19–21 as the letter's turn toward the prophetic word. It has used Acts 1:22 as a qualification of seeing and left the authority of the college in its place. It has noted Luke 24's opening of the Scriptures as belonging to an appearance and left the Graphē-argument in its place.

It has established that the authentic testimony presents positioned witnesses of what was seen and heard concerning Jesus Christ — of His majesty and of His raising — and that this presentation is a central authentication line of Movement VI at this stage.

Local questions of how a particular appearance-scene was remembered, of the literary relationship among the Synoptic Transfiguration accounts, of the precise history of 2 Peter's composition, and of the exact mapping of every named seer onto every hour remain as local questions. They are not a global rival. They do not reopen the definition. They do not convert 2 Peter 1:16–18 into a maybe. They do not restore mere presence, later commentary, legend, hallucination, or collusion as adequate accounts of the conjunction.

One scope statement is enough. The force of the authentication line is not diminished by the existence of later chapters.

# 47.46 Apply the Standard

The reader should now be able to take any proposed sentence about "witnesses of Jesus" and ask:

> **Is this sentence a claim of historical existence, of identity with the Truth, of claims-and-works authentication, of death-and-resurrection as hinge, of eyewitness as positioned knowledge, or of a reserved file of Scripture-confirmation or apostolic office?**

Then:

> **If it is an eyewitness sentence, is it positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard, or is it mere presence, or later commentary, or testimony of another species?**

Then:

> **Does the proposed reduction explain 2 Peter 1:16–18, the Synoptic Transfiguration, 1 John 1:1–3, Luke 1:1–4, 1 Corinthians 15:5–8, the tomb-women, and Acts 2:32 together, or only a preferred strand?**

Then:

> **Is the conclusion being postponed because later chapters remain, or is it being drawn at the level the grounds support?**

If the grounds are the authentic testimony's explicit seeing and hearing, attached to the historical Person already identified as the Truth, already authenticated in the ministry, and already examined at the hinge, with the reductions failing, the eyewitness line is to be granted with full force.

If a later conclusion is desired — that He confirms Scripture, that apostolic testimony carries His authority as office — it is to be sought in its chapter, not smuggled into the mountain and the tomb and not used to postpone the seers.

If a catalogue of "eyewitness proofs" mixes Peter's mountain-claim with later pious legend and with the virtue of the churches, the catalogue is to be classified before it is allowed to speak of this line. Peter can warrant a first-person seeing-claim of majesty. A later homily cannot become an ἐπόπτης by being devout. Classification is the discipline of the whole book.

The governing maxim remains:

> **Do not make the reader choose between reason and Scripture. Teach the reader to reason through Scripture.**

Reasoning through the writings at this stage, concerning the Person already located, identified, authenticated, and examined at the hinge, yields eyewitness testimony as a central authentication line of Movement VI. That is not the abandonment of historical method. It is the refusal to separate what the record joins, and the refusal to call that joining a postponement.

# 47.47 From Eyewitness Testimony to Christ's Confirmation of Scripture

The seers have been examined as seers. The mountain has been heard. The appearances have been taken as witnessing of the risen Christ. The women have been given their place. The named lists stand.

The same scenes, and the same writings, do not leave the Graphē untouched. 2 Peter 1:19 turns from eyewitness of majesty to a more sure word of prophecy, to which the readers do well to take heed. Luke 24 records that the raised Lord opens Moses, the prophets, and the psalms as concerning Himself. The earliest formula says "according to the scriptures." Acts 2 argues from what is written. The authentic testimony's seers are seers of a Person who Himself treats writings as authoritative.

That is not yet Chapter 48.

The next necessary question is not a new curiosity. It is the question the seers' own Lord forces. If He is the Truth, if His works authenticate His claims, if death and raising are the hinge, if positioned witnesses saw His majesty and His raising, then His own treatment of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative is the next object. Seeing Him is not yet His verdict on what is written. His verdict on what is written is the next authentication axis of Movement VI.

The question is therefore not:

> **Is eyewitness testimony positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard concerning this Person, and does that testimony function as a central authentication line?**

That question has been answered.

The question is:

> **How did this Person treat the Scriptures He received, and what does His confirmation of those writings establish now that He has been located, identified, authenticated, examined at the hinge, and attested by seers?**

That question is not a retreat from the seers. It is the seers' Lord examined in His relation to the writings. The investigation therefore moves from:

> **We were eyewitnesses of His majesty; He was seen; we are witnesses of what we have seen and heard.**

to:

> **What did He confirm as written, and with what force?**

That is the proper open of the next chapter of Movement VI. The eyewitness line was never meant to be the last word. It was meant to be a word sufficient to justify taking the next one, which is the word the raised Lord Himself placed in the seers' ears on the road and in the room: what is written.

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 47 established that the historical Person of Chapter 43, already identified in Chapter 44 as the Truth and the decisive revealer of the Father, already presented in Chapter 45 as one whose public claims and public works belong together as a central authentication axis, already examined in Chapter 46 at the hinge of death and resurrection, was seen and heard by positioned witnesses: not mere presence, and not later commentary. 2 Peter 1:16–18 grounded that category. The appearances were taken as eyewitness events of the risen Christ. The women, the disciples, and the named lists were given their force. That eyewitness line is already in force.

Chapter 47 ended by naming the next necessary question, not a new curiosity:

> **How did Jesus Christ treat the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative, and what does that confirmation establish now that the seers of His majesty and of His raising have been examined?**

That is this chapter's assignment.

The locked Table of Contents states the work in one sentence:

> **Examine Christ's treatment of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative.**

The chapter does not re-prove historical existence. It cites Chapter 43 as established. It does not re-argue identity with the Truth. It cites Chapter 44 as established. It does not re-try the claims-and-works conjunction. It cites Chapter 45 as established. It does not re-try the death-and-resurrection case. It cites Chapter 46 as established. It does not re-try the seers as a dedicated credibility-file. It cites Chapter 47 as established. It does not consummate Christ and the apostolic witness. It does not close the authority of apostolic testimony as a finished argument of office. It does not construct a canon list. It does not pronounce the infallibility verdict. It does not treat John 10:34–36 as finished Graphē-doctrine. It does not treat John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine. It does not claim that the Graphē is primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. It performs the examination without which those later investigations would be investigations of a named, authenticated, raised, and attested Person whose relation to the writings already in force had then been left unnamed as a file.

A Person who is the Truth still stands under writings that preceded His public ministry. Identity does not abolish those writings. It makes His treatment of them the treatment of the Truth. The writings that have now been used as authentic testimony do not stop at the seers. They present this man as quoting what is written in temptation, as asking whether His hearers have not read, as opening a synagogue scroll and claiming fulfillment, as refusing to destroy the Law and the Prophets, as charging error to those who do not know the Scriptures, as joining His passion to what the prophets wrote, and, after the raising, as opening Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning Himself. Those are further claims about the same career. They are the claims for which a historical baseline, a revelatory identification, an authentication axis, a hinge of death and raising, and a file of seers now exist.

The remaining questions of Movement VI follow by sequence. Sequence continues the investigation. It does not convert the present line into hesitation.

## Central Objective

> **To define Christ's confirmation of Scripture, in this argument, as His treatment of already-written Holy Writ as binding written word — received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative; to distinguish that object from optional illustration, from canon-list construction, from the infallibility verdict, from Movement VIII's finished Graphē-doctrine, and from the apostolic files of Chapters 49–50; to examine representative passages in their contexts rather than as a slogan list; to expose the reductions that fail; and to state, with full force, that this confirmation is a central authentication line of Movement VI in the sense this chapter defines.**

The governing movement is:

> **Seers already in force → question of His treatment of the writings → definition of confirmation as authoritative handling of received Scripture → distinctions that protect the object → Law, Prophets, and Psalms as the body He names → the language of what stands written → temptation citations → “have you not read” → synagogue reading → not destroy but fulfill → the Scriptures as witnesses concerning Him → fulfillment in the passion → Emmaus and the opened writings → failure of reductions → inspectable inference → warranted authentication line → sequence to Christ and the apostolic witness.**

The chapter's conclusion is affirmative:

> **Jesus Christ, already established as a historical figure of the early first century, already identified as the Truth and the revealer of the Father, already authenticated in the ministry's claims-and-works conjunction, already examined at the hinge of death and raising, and already attested by positioned witnesses of what was seen and heard, is presented by the authentic written testimony as one who received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to the Scriptures already written — Law, Prophets, and Psalms — as authoritative written word, not as optional illustration. “It is written” is His formula of force in conflict. “Have ye not read” is His assumption that the written text settles what is in dispute. The synagogue reading is a public claim that a written prophet is fulfilled in the hearers' ears. The raised Lord opens Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning Himself. Confirmation of the Scriptures He received is not yet the finished Movement VIII verdict that the scripture cannot be broken, not yet John 17:17 as Graphē-doctrine, not yet canon, not yet infallibility, and not yet the Graphē as primary written authority. The authentic testimony's positive case is that this Person confirmed the writings He received as binding written word. That case is a central authentication line of Movement VI, stated here with full force.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The authentication line is already in force.

# 48.1 The Question Created by the Preceding Chapter

Movement VI has located a Person, identified Him as the Truth, examined His public claims and works as an authentication axis, taken His death and resurrection as the central historical claims of the career's end, and examined the seers of His majesty and of His raising as positioned witnesses. It has not yet examined His treatment of the writings already in force.

Chapter 43 established existence, publicity, chronology, Jewish setting, crucifixion under Pilate, and the failure of myth and coreless legend. Chapter 44 established identity with the Truth and decisive revelation of the Father. Chapter 45 established the claims-and-works conjunction as a central authentication axis. Chapter 46 established crucifixion as the public end of that ministry, burial as a belonging fact, and resurrection as the early, bodily, public, appearance-claim of the same testimony. Chapter 47 established eyewitness testimony as positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard. Those conclusions are premises here.

A Person can be located, identified, authenticated in the ministry, examined at the hinge of death and raising, and attested by seers, and a further question still remains: how did this Person treat the Scriptures He received? Identity that never stands under prior writings is not the identity the Gospels present. A raised Lord who never opens Moses and the prophets is not the Lord Luke 24 presents. The writings that have now been used as authentic testimony do not stop at “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty.” They record this man answering temptation with what is written, rebuking error as ignorance of the Scriptures, reading a prophet in the synagogue of His upbringing, claiming not to destroy the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them, and, after the raising, beginning at Moses and all the prophets and expounding in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself. Those are further claims about the same career. They are the claims for which a historical baseline, a revelatory identification, an authentication axis, a hinge, and a file of seers now exist.

The question is therefore not:

> **Did a man named Jesus occupy Galilee and Judea under Tiberius, is He presented as the Truth, do His claims and works function as an authentication axis, are death and resurrection the central historical claims of the career's end, and are there positioned witnesses of what was seen and heard?**

Those questions have been answered.

The question is:

> **How did this Person treat the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative, and what does that treatment warrant now that the object of the investigation is this Person's confirmation of those writings?**

If citation stood alone as ornament, Movement VI would be the investigation of a preacher's stock of phrases. If later church use of the Old Testament stood alone, Movement VI would be the investigation of Christian midrash after the fact. If this Person treats the received writings as binding written word, Movement VI is the investigation of the Truth's own confirmation of the Scriptures already in force.

That is a different operation from piety. It is the operation this chapter must perform.

# 48.2 What This Chapter Does Not Repeat

Chapter 20 established γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Scripture / Holy Writ. Chapter 21 examined that lexical field in the New Testament's appeals to what is written. Chapter 22 distinguished Graphē, Holy Writ, Scripture, Bible, and written Word. Those definitions are premises. This chapter does not re-try the lexicon. It uses it.

Chapter 26 established, from the biblical record as a mode of giving, that Jesus Christ occupies a unique and climactic place: the Son, the Word made flesh, the revelation of the Father. It recorded, as a preliminary observation, that He appeals to Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, that He reasons from Scripture, and that Luke 24 presents Him explaining the things concerning Himself in those writings. It reserved the dedicated examination of that treatment as Movement VI's later assignment. That reservation is now due.

Chapter 30 established inspiration as the biblical doctrine of Scripture's production, with 2 Timothy 3:15–17 as the governing text. Chapter 31 refused to weaken “all Scripture.” Those conclusions stand. This chapter does not re-argue inspiration. It examines Christ's handling of writings already treated in the record as Scripture.

Chapter 37 established prophecy and fulfillment as an evidential category, with the required marks of specificity, priority, and correspondence. It noted New Testament use of earlier texts concerning Jesus without making Jesus' own handling of those texts its dedicated object. This chapter does not re-try the predictive-correspondence case. It examines His confirmation of the writings as authoritative, including His own use of fulfillment-language.

Chapter 38 established unity and continuity across the corpus, including the claim that Jesus came not to destroy the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them. Continuity of the writings is not identical with this Person's confirmation of them as His own practice. The former is a property of the corpus. The latter is an act of the central witness.

Chapter 42 established the warrant to treat the biblical writings as authentic written testimony of the claims under investigation. That warrant is a premise. This chapter does not re-open Movement V.

Chapters 43–47 established the Person, the identity, the authentication axis, the hinge, and the seers. Those conclusions are premises.

This chapter does not re-try Tacitus and Josephus as if existence were still in doubt. It does not recatalogue Capernaum. It does not re-argue whether the resurrection claim is bodily, public, and a claim of appearances. It does not convert 2 Peter 1:16–18 into a substitute for His handling of what is written. It does not treat Acts 1:22 as the finished argument of apostolic office. It does not treat John 10:34–36 as the finished verdict that the scripture cannot be broken. The new function is this:

> **To isolate Christ's confirmation of the Scriptures He received as the next necessary question about the One already identified as the Truth, already authenticated in the ministry, already examined at the hinge, and already attested by seers, using the writings as the authentic testimony of how He treated what was already written, and to state what that confirmation warrants before Movement VI develops the apostolic witness and its authority.**

# 48.3 Define the Question: Confirmation as Authoritative Treatment of Received Writings

**Confirmation**, in this chapter, is Christ's treatment of already-written Scripture as binding written word.

The object is not a later ecclesiastical certificate. It is not a list of books. It is not a metaphysical verdict that every sentence of a later closed corpus is incapable of error. It is this Person's practice, in the authentic testimony, of receiving, quoting, interpreting, and appealing to the writings already in force as authoritative.

Four acts belong to the definition.

First, **reception**. He enters a people already possessed of writings. He is a Jew of Galilee and Judea under the Second Temple, as Chapter 43 established. Those writings are read in synagogues. They are the Law, the Prophets, and, in His own later naming, the Psalms. He does not invent the corpus He uses. He receives it.

Second, **quotation**. He cites what is written as written. The ordinary formula is **γέγραπται (*gegraptai*)**: it stands written. The citation is not an allusion that might as well have been a proverb. It is an appeal to a text.

Third, **interpretation**. He reads, explains, applies, and, after the raising, opens the writings concerning Himself. Interpretation is not the abolition of the text. It is the act of a mind upon a text treated as having force. The hermeneutical discipline of later Movements IX–X is not this chapter's assignment. The fact that He interprets, and that He interprets the writings as concerning Himself and as binding upon His hearers, belongs here.

Fourth, **appeal as authoritative**. He does not offer the writings as optional colour. He uses them as the court of appeal in temptation, in controversy, in the synagogue, in the passion, and in the post-resurrection instruction. “Have ye not read” is not a literary compliment. It is a charge that the written text was available and decisive.

**Central authentication line**, in this chapter, names the function of that confirmation inside Movement VI. The locked TOC assigns this chapter Christ's treatment of the Scriptures He received, quoted, interpreted, and appealed to as authoritative. The assignment is therefore not a free selection of pious Old Testament scenes. It is the examination of what the record places as this Person's own relation to the writings already in force.

The question of this chapter joins those definitions:

> **Does the authentic testimony present this Person as receiving, quoting, interpreting, and appealing to the Scriptures already written as binding written word, such that that confirmation functions as a central authentication line of Movement VI?**

Several elements belong to the question as this chapter defines it.

First, **the body He names**. Law, Prophets, and Psalms are His own grouping of the received writings, not a later scholar's convenience.

Second, **the formula of force**. “It is written,” “have ye not read,” “this scripture,” “the scriptures,” and “that the scriptures might be fulfilled” are the record's own names for the operation.

Third, **representative passages in context**. Temptation, synagogue reading, controversy over reading, the claim not to destroy but to fulfill, the Scriptures as witnesses concerning Him, the passion's necessity as written, and the Emmaus and upper-room openings are examined as arguments, not as a slogan list.

Fourth, **examinability**. These are claims inside a warranted written testimony about a historical Person. They can be defined, distinguished, compared with reductions, and reasoned through. They are not exempt from investigation because they are theological. They are not reduced to later church policy because they are Jewish.

Thus:

> **The question of Christ's confirmation of Scripture is the question of His authoritative treatment of the writings He received, under the writings already warranted as testimony, with Law, Prophets, and Psalms as the named body, and with “it is written” as a formula of force rather than of decoration.**

# 48.4 Distinguish Seven Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats seven different objects as one.

## 48.4.1 Historical existence, identity, claims-and-works, the hinge, and the seers

These are the objects of Chapters 43–47. They include a real person, identity with the Truth, the public authentication axis of claims and works, death-and-resurrection as the central historical claims of the career's end, and eyewitness testimony as positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard. Those conclusions are premises here. This chapter does not re-try them. It examines this Person's treatment of the writings so established.

## 48.4.2 Confirmation of received Scripture as authoritative written word

This is the object of the present chapter. It includes: the definition of confirmation as reception, quotation, interpretation, and authoritative appeal; Law, Prophets, and Psalms as the body He names; the language of what stands written; temptation, reading, synagogue, fulfillment, controversy, passion, and the opened writings after the raising; the failure of specified reductions; and the warrant for treating this confirmation as a central authentication line of Movement VI.

## 48.4.3 Optional illustration

A teacher may quote a famous sentence because it is memorable. Illustration borrows light. Confirmation treats the text as binding. Collapsing the two converts “it is written” into décor. The record's use of the formula in conflict, in rebuke, and in the necessity of the passion is not décor.

## 48.4.4 Canon-list construction

Canon, in this book's architecture, is the question of which writings constitute the recognized authoritative scriptural corpus. That question is Movement VII. A man may confirm the writings He uses without issuing a catalogue of titles, without adjudicating disputed edges, and without performing the later church's recognition-history. Confirmation of received Scripture is not a list. Movement VII remains the list's proper file.

## 48.4.5 Infallibility as a finished verdict

Infallibility, in this book's architecture, is the conclusion concerning the truthfulness and reliability of the inspired record, built from premises concerning God, revelation, inspiration, authentication, and Scripture. That conclusion is Movement VII's later work, especially Chapters 56–57. Treating the writings as authoritative is not yet the metaphysical verdict that the later closed corpus is an infallible record. The present chapter may not steal that verdict by renaming confirmation as infallibility.

## 48.4.6 Movement VIII's finished Graphē-doctrine

John 10:34–36, “the scripture cannot be broken,” Christ's reasoning from the written wording of Psalm 82:6, John 17:17 as “thy word is truth,” and the conclusion that the Graphē is the primary written authority are the locked assignments of Chapters 59–65. He does appeal to what is written in John 10. That appeal is noted here as an instance of the same practice. The dedicated argument of why Scripture cannot be broken, and the Graphē-gate that follows, remain Movement VIII. Confirmation of received Scripture is the Movement VI line. The later verdict is the later verdict.

## 48.4.7 Apostolic witness and the authority of apostolic testimony

Chapter 49 examines Christ's relationship to the apostles and the authority of their testimony concerning Him. Chapter 50 establishes why apostolic testimony is relevant to authentication of the New Testament witness and its relationship to earlier Scripture. Those are the remaining files of Movement VI. This chapter's object is His treatment of the writings already in force, not yet the college He sends, and not yet the authority of their testimony as a finished argument of office.

The seven objects may be named together in a sentence. They may not be treated as one object. The present chapter examines the second.

# 48.5 Premises That May Be Used, and Premises That May Not

The following premises may be used because they have been earned.

1. The biblical writings are authentic written testimony of the claims under investigation (Movement V, especially Chapter 42).
2. γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) denotes writing, and in the relevant biblical usage denotes Scripture / Holy Writ (Chapters 20–22).
3. Jesus Christ occupies a unique and climactic place in divine revelation as the Son and the Word made flesh (Chapter 26). That chapter's preliminary notice of His use of Scripture is a pointer, not this file's substitute.
4. Inspiration as the biblical doctrine of Scripture's production has been examined (Chapters 30–31). This chapter does not re-prove it and does not convert it into Movement VIII's gate.
5. Prophecy and fulfillment is a real evidential category with specified marks (Chapter 37). This chapter does not re-try that case.
6. Jesus of Nazareth is a historical person of the early first century, a Jew of Galilee and Judea, publicly active, crucified under Pontius Pilate (Chapter 43).
7. He is identified as the Truth and the decisive revealer of the Father (Chapter 44).
8. His public claims and public works function as a central authentication axis (Chapter 45).
9. Death and resurrection are the central historical claims of the career's end (Chapter 46). “According to the scriptures” belongs to the earliest formula as the formula's own clause.
10. Eyewitness testimony is positioned knowledge of what was seen and heard (Chapter 47). 2 Peter 1:19–21 was left as the letter's turn toward the prophetic word. That turn may now be named as belonging to the present file's neighbourhood, without becoming the finished doctrine of inspiration.

The following premises may not be used, because they have not been earned as finished conclusions, or because they belong to later chapters.

1. That the Graphē is the primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense (Chapter 65).
2. That “the scripture cannot be broken” has been examined as finished doctrine (Chapters 59–63).
3. That John 17:17 has been examined as finished Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
4. That a closed canon list has been constructed from His quotations (Movement VII).
5. That infallibility has been pronounced as a finished verdict (Chapters 56–57).
6. That apostolic testimony carries His authority as a closed case of office (Chapters 49–50).
7. That the Six First Principles have been entered, or that σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704) has been developed as Movement X's labour (Chapters 78, 85).
8. That Christianity as institutional label, later councils, or later confessions may be treated as the measure of His practice.

The argument is therefore not:

> **The Bible is God's Word; Jesus is God; therefore whatever He quoted is infallible Scripture; therefore the canon is closed.**

That compression steals Movements VII and VIII. The argument is:

> **The writings are warranted as authentic testimony. The Person is located, identified, authenticated, examined at the hinge, and attested by seers. That Person treats the writings He received as binding written word. That confirmation is a central authentication line of Movement VI at this stage.**

Circularity would be the use of this confirmation to assume the Graphē-gate while pretending to open it. Sequence is the refusal of that circle.

# 48.6 Confirmation Defined: Receive, Quote, Interpret, Appeal

The four acts named in the definition must be stated as operations, not as synonyms for piety.

**To receive** the Scriptures, in this argument, is to stand inside a people for whom those writings already function as Holy Writ, and to take them as given rather than as optional background. Reception is historical before it is homiletical. A Galilean Jew of the late Second Temple inherits Moses, the prophets, and the psalms as public writings. He is presented as hearing them, reading them, and treating them as the writings of that people. Reception is not passivity. It is the first act of confirmation: the writings are not a foreign library He happens to find useful.

**To quote** is to cite a writing as writing. The perfect **γέγραπται (*gegraptai*)** is the ordinary Synoptic form: it has been written, and the writing remains. Quotation in this sense is not the later scholar's footnote. It is speech that treats a prior sentence as present force. When He answers, “It is written,” the cited sentence is being used as the rule of the present conflict.

**To interpret** is to say what the writing means in the situation before Him. He reads Isaiah in the synagogue and claims the day of fulfillment. He asks what David means by calling the Messiah Lord. He begins at Moses and the prophets and expounds the things concerning Himself. Interpretation can be true or false. This chapter does not close the later hermeneutical discipline. It establishes that He interprets, and that He interprets writings He treats as having the right to bind.

**To appeal as authoritative** is to treat the writing as the court before which a dispute is to be settled, a temptation is to be answered, a charge is to be made, or a necessity is to be named. Authority here is not yet the Movement VIII thesis that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which all later claims are tested. It is the more precise and already sufficient claim that, in His practice, the received writings function as binding written word.

The four acts are one confirmation. Reception without quotation would be atmosphere. Quotation without appeal would be ornament. Appeal without interpretation would be talisman. Interpretation without reception would be invention. The record presents the four together.

---

# 48.7 Illustration Is Not Confirmation

A sentence may be quoted because it is beautiful, familiar, or useful as a comparison. Illustration does not treat the quoted sentence as the rule of the case. Confirmation does.

The distinction is not an accusation against all metaphor. Jesus speaks in parables. He uses comparisons. Those forms are not this chapter's object. The object is the class of acts in which He names what is written as written and uses it as decisive.

Three marks separate illustration from confirmation in the passages this chapter examines.

First, **the formula names writing**. “It is written,” “have ye not read,” “this scripture,” “the law,” “Moses,” “the prophets,” “the psalms,” “that which was spoken unto you by God” — these are designations of a prior written or God-spoken-and-written word, not of a free image.

Second, **the use is adjudicative**. In temptation the cited word is the refusal of the proposed act. In controversy the cited word is the exposure of error. In the passion the cited word is the necessity: thus it must be. Illustration does not ordinarily carry necessity.

Third, **the hearers are held responsible for the text**. “Have ye not read” assumes that reading was the available act and that failure to read, or failure to regard what was read, is the error. A mere illustration does not generate that charge.

The reduction that treats all citation as illustration therefore fails at the formula, at the adjudicative use, and at the charge. Confirmation is the right name for the operation the record exhibits.

---

# 48.8 Confirmation Distinguished from Canon-List Construction

A list of books is one kind of intellectual act. Confirmation of writings in use is another.

Jesus quotes Moses, Isaiah, the Psalms, Daniel, Hosea, and other writings of the received Jewish Scriptures. He names “the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms” as the body of things written concerning Himself (Luke 24:44). That naming is a grouping of received writings. It is not a canon-synod. It does not enumerate Esther. It does not adjudicate the later Christian disputes about the edges of the corpus. It does not, by silence, automatically exclude every writing He does not happen to cite in the recorded scenes.

Two errors must be refused together.

The first error is **inflation**. Inflation says: He quoted these books; therefore He issued the later Protestant or Jewish list; therefore Movement VII is already finished. Quotation is not a synod. Grouping Law, Prophets, and Psalms is a real confirmation of a received body. It is not the later recognition-history.

The second error is **evacuation**. Evacuation says: because He did not print a catalogue, He confirmed nothing. The absence of a later list-form is not the absence of authoritative treatment. A man who lives by what is written, reads the prophet in the synagogue, and opens Moses and the prophets after His raising has confirmed writings. He has not thereby performed Movement VII.

The Bible Introduction's observation that the Jewish Scriptures were divided as Law, Prophets, and Writings, and that Christ referred to this division as the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, is a historical correspondence worth stating as correspondence. The correspondence supports reception of a known body. It does not license this chapter to settle which later titles belong at the edges. Movement VII remains the file of corpus and recognition.

---

# 48.9 Confirmation Distinguished from Infallibility Verdict

Infallibility, as this book will later argue it, concerns what follows from God's truthfulness, from genuine revelation, from inspiration, and from authentication, for the truthfulness of the inspired written record. That argument has unfinished premises. God as the ground of truth, and the impossibility of God's lying, have been established in Movement II. Inspiration has been examined as a doctrine of production. Authentication is still accumulating. Canon has not been examined. The Graphē-gate has not been drawn.

Confirmation is an act of this Person toward writings He received. The act has evidential force because of who He has already been shown to be. It does not, by itself, pronounce the later verdict that the completed corpus is an infallible record.

The distinction protects both conclusions. If confirmation is quietly renamed infallibility, Movement VII becomes a repetition. If confirmation is refused any force until infallibility is pronounced, Movement VI is emptied of the line the TOC assigns it. The writings He treats as binding written word are confirmed by the Truth as binding written word. That is already a central authentication line. The later verdict will ask why those writings, as Graphē, cannot be broken. Different question. Later chapter.

---

# 48.10 Confirmation Distinguished from Movement VIII's Finished Graphē-Doctrine

John 10:34–36 records a controversy in which Jesus answers an accusation of blasphemy by citing what is written in the Law: “I said, Ye are gods.” He then says that the scripture cannot be broken, and reasons from the written wording to His own consecration and sending. That scene is an instance of the practice this chapter examines: He appeals to what is written as written, and He treats the written wording as having force that His argument may not evade.

The scene is not this chapter's dedicated object.

The locked TOC assigns John 10:34–36, Psalm 82:6, Christ's reasoning from what is written, “the scripture cannot be broken,” the why of that statement, John 17:17, and the Graphē as primary written authority to Chapters 59–65. Those chapters exist because the argument of John 10 is an argument, not a slogan, and because the why of “cannot be broken” must rest on what Scripture is, not merely on the fact that Jesus quoted it.

This chapter therefore records the practice and reserves the verdict. He confirms received Scripture by treating the written wording as decisive in controversy. Movement VIII will ask why that wording cannot be broken, and what follows for the Graphē as primary written authority. The reservation is sequence. It is not a suspicion that John 10 is weak. It is the refusal to steal the later why.

John 17:17 — “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” — is likewise reserved. The present chapter's object is His treatment of the received writings as authoritative written word. The later chapter's object is the relation of God's Word to truth as Graphē-doctrine. The sentences are neighbours. They are not the same assignment.
